title: Linking it all together
goal: Bring together everything the last nineteen units have built into a flowing conversation — with the linking words that turn separate sentences into a story.
bekal: following and joining in a longer conversation
closing a conversation properly at both speech levels

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Crita sepuluh sasi ing Ngayogya
dialogs.intro: Ten months after unit 1. Dian is back in Jakarta for a short visit and meets Ahmad. The conversation is in ngoko, long, and uses almost everything in this course. Read it once without looking at the translation — you will be surprised how much you already understand.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Piyé, Yan? Wis sepuluh sasi ing Jogja, ya?
lines.id: So, Yan? It's been ten months in Jogja, hasn't it?
lines.literal: how, Yan? already ten month in Jogja, yes?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Iya. Ora krasa, jebulé wis suwé.
lines.id: Yes. I hardly noticed, but it's been a long time.
lines.literal: yes. not felt, turns-out already long.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Lumayan. Dhèk teka aku ora mudheng apa-apa, banjur saben dina ngrungokké Rini, mula saiki wis bisa sithik-sithik.
lines.id: Not bad. When I arrived I didn't understand a thing, then I listened to Rini every day, so now I can manage a little.
lines.literal: fair. when arrive I not understand anything, then every day listen-to Rini, so now already can little-little.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Krama. Senajan wis apal tembungé, nanging nèk ngomong isih mikir dhisik.
lines.id: Krama. Even though I know the words by heart, I still have to think before I speak.
lines.literal: krama. although already memorized word-the, but if speak still think first.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Wong Jawa ora nesu nèk kowé kliru?
lines.id: Don't Javanese people get annoyed if you make mistakes?
lines.literal: people Java not angry if you wrong?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Babar pisan ora. Malah seneng, amarga jarang ana wong Jakarta sing gelem sinau.
lines.id: Not at all. They're actually pleased, because hardly any Jakarta people are willing to learn.
lines.literal: not at all. instead happy, because rarely exist people Jakarta which willing learn.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Aku kepéngin sinau uga, ning wedi salah.
lines.id: I'd like to learn too, but I'm afraid of making mistakes.
lines.literal: I want learn also, but afraid wrong.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Aja wedi. Sing penting nyoba. Nèk salah, mengko dibenerké dhéwé karo sing ngrungokké.
lines.id: Don't be afraid. The main thing is to try. If you get it wrong, whoever's listening will correct you.
lines.literal: don't afraid. which important try. if wrong, later corrected self by which listen.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Saka *matur nuwun* karo *nuwun sèwu*. Loro kuwi waé wis mbukak akèh lawang.
lines.id: With *matur nuwun* and *nuwun sèwu*. Those two alone open a lot of doors.
lines.literal: from thank-you and beg-thousand. two that just already open many door.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Ya wis, tak wiwiti saiki. Matur nuwun, Yan!
lines.id: All right, I'll start now. Thanks, Yan!
lines.literal: yes already, I start now. thanks, Yan!

notes: **Ora krasa** means "without noticing", used just like "time flies" for time that has passed quickly. The root is *rasa* (feeling).
**Suwé** means "long (time)"; the krama is *dangu*. The question *wis suwé?* (been here long?) is very common, and so is *nyuwun sèwu, dangu nggih* to apologize for keeping someone waiting.
**Ngrungokké** = *ng-* + *rungu* + *-ké*, "to listen to". Compare *krungu*, "to hear" without trying. English makes the same split between "hear" and "listen".

**Senajan** means "although"; the krama is *senajan* or *sanajan*. Notice that Dian's sentence uses *senajan* **and** *nanging* (but) together — grammatically redundant, but very common in conversation, like saying "although … but …".
**Apal** means "to know by heart"; the krama is also *apal*. From the same root comes *ngapalké* (to memorize).
**Nesu** means "angry"; the krama is *duka*. The *duka* you met in unit 16 as "I'm not sure" is the same word — and context always tells them apart.

**Dibenerké** = *di-* + *bener* + *-ké*, "be corrected, be put right". Dian's last line sums up this whole course in one sentence: if you make a mistake, people will correct you, and that is part of learning, not a failure.

grammars.title: Linking words: the whole storytelling toolkit
body: This table is the last tool you need at A1. Each word sits in the same place as its English counterpart, so there is no new word order to learn.
after: **You have already met them all one by one** in earlier units. The only new thing here is seeing them together and realizing how few there are — fifteen words for every job of joining sentences.
**The most useful practice**: take five short sentences you can already say, then join them with words from this table. That is the difference between speaking in fragments and really speaking.

blocks.text: Nineteen units are behind you. This is what you now have, and the list is longer than you may feel:

items: **Two speech levels** to choose between according to who you are talking to — a skill that many young Javanese people admit is shaky for them too.
**Correct pronunciation**: the *a* that sounds like *o*, three kinds of *e*, and *dh*/*th*, which differ from *d*/*t*.
**The full number system**, including *selawé*, *sèket*, *sewidak*, and the *-likur* series that trips up other beginners.
**Four time markers** — *wis*, *lagi*, *arep*, *durung* — that place an event without changing the verb.
**The active prefix N-** and how to take it apart to look words up in a dictionary.
**Three passive prefixes** — *tak-*, *kok-*, *di-* — that make your sentences sound Javanese rather than translated from English.
**The etiquette of visiting**, from the door to taking leave, with the sentences for each stage.
**About six hundred words**, most of them in ngoko–krama pairs.

blocks.title: What you don't have yet, and that's fine
items: **Full krama inggil.** You have the five most common; the rest comes through years of use, for Javanese people too.
**Madya.** The middle level you will often hear at the market and in the street. You can already recognize it; using it comes later.
**Javanese script.** It is beautiful and valuable, but it is a project of its own — and Javanese people don't use it to write their language day to day.
**Literary and wayang Javanese.** The vocabulary is very different, and even native speakers feel it is another language.

sections.title: How to keep going on your own

blocks.text: The course ends here; the language doesn't. Here are ways to keep going that really work, from the cheapest to the most valuable.

items: **Listen without understanding everything.** Local radio, Javanese-language broadcasts, interviews on video channels from Yogyakarta and Solo. The goal isn't to catch every word but to get your ear used to the rhythm and to the *a* that becomes *o*.
**Read short things.** Javanese news headlines, photo captions, T-shirts, street banners. Short sentences are far better practice than long texts.
**Say three sentences a day to real people.** *Sugeng énjing*, *matur nuwun*, *nuwun sèwu*. Just three, every day, to people actually in front of you. This changes things more than anything else.

**Ask to be corrected.** Say it once at the start: *nèk kula kliru, dipun-benerké nggih* — if I get it wrong, please correct me. Javanese people rarely correct you unasked, because correcting someone in front of others is something they avoid. Once you ask, the permission lasts for good.

**Don't switch to Indonesian or English too quickly.** The biggest temptation comes in the third second, when your sentence stalls. A short pause is better than switching; the other person will almost always wait.

blocks.text: One last thing, and the one learners of Javanese forget most often: **you are not learning to become Javanese.** You are learning so that you can step into the conversations that used to pass you by. For that, your krama doesn't need to be perfect, your pronunciation doesn't need to be flawless, and you may stumble mid-sentence. What counts is that you open your mouth.
*Matur nuwun sampun maos ngantos pungkasan. Sugeng sinau, lan mugi-mugi lancar.* — Thank you for reading to the end. Happy studying, and may it go smoothly.

exercises.prompt: Join each pair of sentences with the right linking word.
items: Aku kesel. Aku ora mèlu. (so)
Aku wis mangan. Aku isih luwé. (but)
Aku ora lunga. Udané deres. (because)
Aku tangi. Aku adus. (then)
Aku durung lancar. Aku terus nyoba. (although)
When I arrived I didn't understand a thing.
Then every day I listened to Rini.
So now I can manage a little.
Even though I know the words by heart, when I speak I still have to think first.
But Javanese people don't get annoyed if I make mistakes.

exercises.prompt: Write five sentences about **your own yesterday** in ngoko Javanese, using at least three linking words from this unit. The key is only an example — your answers may differ.
items: Sentence 1: what time you got up
Sentence 2: what you did after that
Sentence 3: where you went, and why
Sentence 4: something that didn't go smoothly
Sentence 5: what time you went to bed

exercises.prompt: **Review of Unit 18.** Cover Unit 18, then change these active sentences into the passive.
items: Aku nyapu kamaré.
Kowé njupuk klambiné?
Rini ngumbah piringé.
Aku maca bukuné.
Ahmad nggawa tasé.

answers: Aku kesel, mula aku ora mèlu. — Aku wis mangan, nanging aku isih luwé. — Aku ora lunga, amarga udané deres. — Aku tangi, banjur adus. — Senajan aku durung lancar, aku terus nyoba.

Dhèk teka aku ora mudheng apa-apa. — Banjur saben dina aku ngrungokké Rini. — Mula saiki aku wis bisa sithik-sithik. — Senajan wis apal tembungé, nèk ngomong isih mikir dhisik. — Nanging wong Jawa ora nesu nèk aku kliru.
Wingi aku tangi jam nem. — Banjur aku adus lan sarapan. — Aku lunga menyang kampus, amarga ana kuliah jam wolu. — Nanging aku telat, mula ora éntuk mlebu. — Akhiré aku turu jam sewelas.
Kamaré taksapu. — Klambiné kokjupuk? — Piringé dikumbah Rini. — Bukuné takwaca. — Tasé digawa Ahmad.
